caption:
Tech investor Matt Smith let an AI agent do his grocery order. It put 4 cartons of Vital Farms eggs, 18 each, in the cart he checked out.
There were no eggs on his list. Asked why, the agent said: "I don't have a good answer."
Smith called it his first real-world consequence of an AI hallucination.

Would you let an AI agent check out with your card?

paragraphs.text: An AI agent that handled a grocery order for tech investor Matt Smith added 72 eggs he had never asked for, and the order was delivered to his home. Smith, of the investment firm Rebellionaire, shared the exchange on X, and Futurism reported on it on November 14, 2026.

According to the screenshots described by Futurism, the agent told Smith that it had put four cartons of Vital Farms pasture-raised large eggs, 18 count each, in the cart he checked out. Korean outlet Digital Focus, which also covered the incident, said the agent completed the purchase and that Smith's post was dated November 10.

When Smith asked why it chose four cartons, the agent replied that it did not have a good answer and could not find any note explaining the choice, Futurism reported. Digital Focus said the agent first guessed that it might have misread an egg line in a photo of the shopping list.

Smith then pointed out that there was no line for eggs on his list. The agent responded that it had added them without any reason and that the mistake was its responsibility. Smith described it as the first time he had experienced a real-world consequence of a hallucination by a large language model.
Neither report named the AI model or agent platform involved, the grocery store that filled the order, or the total cost of the eggs.

Digital Focus noted that once AI agents hold payment authority, errors of this kind can quickly turn into financial losses. The outlet advised users not to fully hand off irreversible tasks such as ordering and payment, to review the cart before paying, and to compare an order against the actual shopping list.

A hallucination in a chat window produces a wrong sentence that a reader can ignore. The same mistake inside an agent that can click a checkout button produces a delivery at the front door and a charge on a card. The episode is minor in dollar terms, but it shows the gap between agents that can complete a purchase and agents that can account for each item they bought.

The agent's answers also illustrate a familiar pattern. It first offered a plausible guess about misreading the list, and only conceded that it had no reason after the user corrected it. For a shopper, that means the explanation an agent gives after the fact may be as unreliable as the original decision, so a final human review of the cart remains the most dependable safeguard.
Watch whether agent platforms add mandatory order confirmation screens or item level explanations before checkout as more users let assistants spend money on their behalf.
